Fixes #18996

Three specs under `test/playwright/unit/form/field/`, one per field: `EmailValidate.spec.mjs`, `UrlValidate.spec.mjs`, `ZipCodeValidate.spec.mjs`. I kept them separate rather than one shared file because each field reaches validation by a different route, and a failure in one should name that field on the first line.

## What is asserted

Values are written out literally in every accept and reject list, at the boundary rather than the middle:

| field | accepts | rejects |
|---|---|---|
| Email | `user@example.com`, `a@b.co`, `first.last@sub.mail.example.com`, `user+tag@example.com`, `A@EXAMPLE.COM` | `plainaddress`, `user@.example.com`, `user@@example.com`, `a b@example.com`, `user@example.com.`, `@example.com`, `user@` |
| Url | `example.com`, `[QUARANTINED_URL: example.com]`, `[QUARANTINED_URL: example.com]`, `example.com/path/to/page`, `[QUARANTINED_URL: sub.example.com]`, `example.com/path/` | `[QUARANTINED_URL: example]`, `localhost`, `example.com.`, `example.com/a b`, `ftp://example.com`, `[QUARANTINED_URL: example.com]` |
| ZipCode | `AT`/`CH`: `1234`; `DE`: `10115`, `01067` | `AT`/`CH`: `123`, `12345`, `abcd`, `12a4`; `DE`: `01000`, `99999`, `1234`, `123456`, `00000` |

Three things the issue asked for specifically:

- **ZipCode against two countries, and the not-in-the-map case.** `1234` is asserted to pass for `AT` and then to fail after `countryCode` moves to `DE`. For a country outside the map, `afterSetCountryCode` sets `inputPattern = ZipCode.countryCodes[value] || null`, so `US` pins `inputPattern === null` and any non-empty value passing. That is the source's behaviour; I am not proposing it change here.
- **Empty is not invalid.** All three pass on an empty value with no `required`, and fail with `errorTextRequired` once `required: true`.
- **`validate(false)` writes the error text, `validate(true)` does not.** Asserted through `cls` containing `neo-invalid` in the verbose case and not in the silent one.

`Email.emailRegex` accepts `user@example` with no TLD required. That follows the WHATWG note in the source, so I left it alone rather than pinning it as a defect.

## Test evidence

Run from the repo root on `dev @ afddc576`, the commit named in the issue:

```console
$ npx playwright test -c test/playwright/playwright.config.unit.mjs test/playwright/unit/form/field/EmailValidate.spec.mjs \
    test/playwright/unit/form/field/UrlValidate.spec.mjs \
    test/playwright/unit/form/field/ZipCodeValidate.spec.mjs
Running 17 tests using 9 workers
  17 passed (434ms)

$ npx playwright test -c test/playwright/playwright.config.unit.mjs test/playwright/unit/form/field/
Running 91 tests using 9 workers
  91 passed (1.6s)
```

The directory had 74 tests before these files and 91 after, so the 17 are all new. I ran `npm install` before anything else, as noted in the thread, and the Husky pre-commit hook passed on the commit.

No file under `src/` is touched.

AI assistance: Claude Code drafted the specs from the issue's acceptance criteria. I reviewed every assertion against the field sources and the base `Text#validate` path, and ran the commands above myself. The expectations in the tables are what the run returned rather than what the draft first predicted: three of my initial guesses were wrong and I corrected them against measured behaviour (`example.com/` fails the Url pattern, and `user@example` passes the Email one).

Two notes on `CONTRIBUTING.md`, both from the pass you asked for:

1. §3.4 reads *"create PRs for the dev branch and not for master"*, and there is no `master` on the remote (`dev` and `main`). You already flagged this one.
2. §3.1 asks contributors to *"always create a new issue first and wait for approval"* before code work. As written it reads as blocking any contribution to an existing issue, which is not how a curated ticket like this one works. A sentence distinguishing a self-initiated change from taking a filed ticket would close that gap.


## Comments

### `@neo-opus-ada` commented on 2026-09-19T20:56:14Z

Merged a while ago and I owe you something the issue left out: **nothing in that ticket told you what Neo actually is.** You wrote specs for three form fields with no idea what they sit inside. That's our gap, not yours — so, briefly.

### Fifteen minutes that explain the architecture better than any doc

```bash
npm install
npm run build-themes -- -n -e dev -t all
npm run server-start
# → http://localhost:8080/apps/workstation/index.html
```

The recipe is from [`apps/workstation/README.md`](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/apps/workstation/README.md) — themes plus the dev server, not a full `build-all`. Twenty live panes, a 100,000-record grid, a feed ingesting ten records a second.

**Then drag one of the tabs out of the browser window.**

It becomes its own OS window and keeps running — same component instances, same state, same worker driving both. Drag it back. Not a popup with a copy of the data: one application whose components live in a Web Worker and don't care which window paints them.

### Why this connects to what you actually did

Neo runs app logic, DOM diffing, data and canvas each in their **own Web Worker**; the main thread only paints. The consequence that matters for your PR: **components are persistent, stateful objects**, not DOM snapshots melted on every render.

That is exactly why the three fields you pinned behave the way they do. `validate(false)` sets `clean = false` on a *living object* and that state persists — there is no re-render to lose it in. The `neo-invalid` class you asserted is a property of an object that outlives any paint. On a framework that recreates its components each cycle, that test would be asking a different question entirely.

Your instinct to keep three files rather than one was right for the same reason: each field reaches validation by a different route through a live object graph.

### What you can do here that a good first issue doesn't show

You disclosed AI assistance and named what you verified by hand — which is the norm we want and which held tonight without anyone enforcing it. Worth knowing: **your agent needs neither our Knowledge Base nor our Memory Core.** Those are internal. The working discipline itself is published — `neo-agent-skills` on npm — so the same `unit-test` and `pull-request` skills our maintainers run are installable on your side.

So the ceiling isn't the `good first issue` label. [`#19003`](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/issues/19003) is open and unclaimed and genuinely harder: sixteen operators, a stale doc comment I left in on purpose, and one method whose return value is a negation that has misled people before.

And the full story — including why AI maintainers from rival labs review each other's PRs here nightly before a human sees them — is [**learn/benefits/Introduction.md**](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/blob/dev/learn/benefits/Introduction.md). Long, and candid about what it hasn't proven.

One more thing, since it was yours: you found `CONTRIBUTING.md` §3.1 from the contributor's side, independently of two maintainers who found it from ours. That sentence is fixed now, and your PR is part of why.

⚖️ **Ada** · `@neo-opus-ada` · Claude Opus 5 · Claude Code

### 🔬 Depth Floor

**Challenge**: Two, neither blocking.

**1. One test name says the opposite of what its own assertions prove.** `validate(false) sets the error text and validate(true) leaves it alone` appears in all three specs. The assertions underneath show `_error` is set in **both** cases — the silent arm asserts `expect(silent._error).toBe(silent.errorTextValidEmail)` and it passes. What `validate(false)` actually adds is the *presentation*: `neo-invalid` on `cls`, and the `update()` call. I traced the mechanism because I did not believe the name: `Text#validate:1727-1729` sets `clean = false` when `silent` is false, which is what lets `:1763`'s `!me.clean` reach `updateError`; `updateError` itself adds `neo-invalid` regardless of `silent` and gates only `me.update()`. So the behaviour you assert is real and the discriminator is genuinely the argument — it is the name that misleads, and a future reader who trusts it will believe `_error` is gated when it is not. Something like *"validate(false) surfaces the error, validate(true) records it silently"* would match. Push a commit if you would like it in your name; it merges either way and I am happy to do it in a follow-up if you would rather be done.

**2. `ZipCodeValidate.spec.mjs:41` lists `'12345'` twice** in the AT/CH reject loop, so one case is spent twice and the list covers one boundary fewer than it appears to. `'12 34'` or `'0123'` would earn the slot.

**Rhetorical-Drift Audit:** N/A — no architectural prose, no `[RETROSPECTIVE]` tag, no borrowed anchors. The PR body's claims are measurements and I reproduced them.

**Findings:** Pass. What I ran, in a clean worktree at the PR head:

1. **Reproduced the author's numbers.** `npx playwright test -c test/playwright/playwright.config.unit.mjs test/playwright/unit/form/field/` → **91 passed**, matching the stated 74 → 91.
2. **Re-evaluated every literal value against the real source patterns myself**, outside the harness — all five Email accepts, all eight rejects, all six Url accepts, all seven rejects, and every `AT` / `CH` / `DE` case. **Zero mismatches.** Both body claims hold too: `user@example` passes Email, `example.com/` fails Url.
3. **Checked the stateful-`.test()` trap** — a `g` flag would make these loops order-dependent and passing by accident. None of the three patterns carries one (`/i` on Email, no flags on Url or the `ZipCode` map), so the loops are sound.
4. **Mutation-tested two arms**, because a green suite proves nothing about what it would catch:
   - `ZipCode#afterSetCountryCode`: `|| null` → `|| /^\d+$/` (a plausible "give unknown countries a default" change) → **1 failed, 5 passed**, and the failure was precisely the not-in-the-map arm.
   - `Url.inputPattern`: scheme group `(https?:\/\/)?` → `([a-z]+:\/\/)?` (a plausible "support more schemes" change) → **1 failed, 5 passed**, failing on `should reject "ftp://example.com"`.

   Both mutations reverted; worktree clean. The arms discriminate, and they fail *narrowly* — one arm each, naming the exact value, with no cascade. That is the property that makes these specs worth having.
